title.en: History: Outbreak of World War I and Its Aftermath

text.en: Raju's grandfather told him about a great war that began with one shot. "Which war?" he asked.

World War I (1914-1918) was fought between the Allied Powers (Britain, France, Russia, later the USA) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Turkey). Its long-term causes were militarism, the alliance system, imperialism and nationalism.
The immediate cause was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria at Sarajevo in 1914. Trench warfare, new weapons and submarines made the war terrible. The war ended with Germany's defeat in 1918.
The Treaty of Versailles (1919) punished Germany with heavy reparations and loss of land. The League of Nations was formed to keep peace, but the harsh terms left bitterness that helped cause the next war.

Before 1914, Europe looked prosperous yet simmered with imperial rivalry over colonies in Africa and Asia, plus a tense arms race at sea between Britain and Germany.

board.text: Pre-1914: Scramble for Colonies & Arms Race

text.en: Two rival armed camps hardened: the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy faced the Triple Entente of Britain, France and Russia.
Aggressive nationalism inflamed tensions—France longed to recover Alsace-Lorraine, Germany claimed world status, and Slavic groups sought freedom from Austria-Hungary in the Balkans.
The spark struck on 28 June 1914 at Sarajevo, when Bosnian Serb nationalist Gavrilo Princip assassinated Austrian heir Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife.

board.text: 28 June 1914: Sarajevo spark lights the war

text.en: Austria blamed Serbia and declared war; Russia mobilised to defend Serbia, pulling alliance partners into a global conflict within weeks.

board.text: Alliances turn regional spark into world war

text.en: On the Western Front, armies dug hundreds of kilometres of muddy trenches guarded by barbed wire, machine guns, poison gas and early tanks.
Costly battles at Verdun and the Somme killed lakhs for just a few kilometres of ground, while German U-boat submarines sank merchant ships in the Atlantic.

board.text: Verdun, Somme & German U-boats at sea

text.en: On the Eastern Front, Russia suffered heavy defeats, food shortages and mutinies—triggering the 1917 Russian Revolutions and Russia's exit via the Brest-Litovsk Treaty.
In 1917, the United States entered on the Allied side after unrestricted German submarine attacks and the Zimmermann Telegram, tipping fresh troops and finance to the Allies.

board.text: 1917: USA enters to tip Allied balance

text.en: India made a crucial Allied contribution too—over 1.3 million Indian soldiers served across Europe, East Africa and West Asia, strengthening India's call for self-rule afterward.

board.text: 1.3 million Indian soldiers served in WWI

text.en: Facing blockade, hunger and revolts at home, Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated, and Germany signed the Armistice on 11 November 1918.
Four old empires collapsed at war's end: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires broke up into new European and West Asian states.
In 1919, victors met at Paris, dominated by the Big Four—Woodrow Wilson (USA), Lloyd George (Britain), Clemenceau (France) and Orlando (Italy).

board.text: 1919 Paris Peace Conference: The Big Four

text.en: While US President Wilson proposed his idealistic Fourteen Points, Britain and France insisted on punishing Germany through the Treaty of Versailles.
Versailles forced Germany to surrender territories and colonies, slash its army, accept sole war guilt under Clause 231, and pay crippling gold reparations.

board.text: Treaty of Versailles: war guilt & reparations

text.en: Meanwhile, Tamil Nadu and all India felt wartime inflation, salt taxes and broken British promises of Swaraj—sparking the Jallianwala Bagh outrage and Gandhi's mass movement.

board.text: WWI impact on India's freedom struggle

text.en: In 1920, the League of Nations was set up in Geneva with an Assembly, Council and International Court to resolve disputes peacefully.

board.text: 1920: League of Nations born in Geneva

text.en: Although the League settled minor border disputes and promoted worker rights through the ILO, it lacked an army—and the USA never even joined.

board.text: Why the League stayed structurally weak

text.en: In defeated Turkey, Mustafa Kemal Ataturk resisted harsh partition and founded a modern, secular republic in 1923.

board.text: Ataturk builds a modern secular Turkey

text.en: Across Europe, wounded soldiers, lost colonies and astronomical war debts bred resentment that extremists later exploited.
Compare causes neatly: M.A.I.N.—Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism and Nationalism—plus the immediate Sarajevo spark.
Follow the causal chain: rival blocs + Balkan crisis -> total industrialised war -> collapse of 4 empires -> harsh Versailles peace.
World War I showed that secret alliances and vengeful treaties never secure lasting peace—a hard lesson remembered when building the UN in 1945.

board.text: Harsh treaties cannot build lasting peace
